source_text: Ne quid enim arduum et inaccessum homini praecipere videretur, verbum de consuetudine usurpavit, ut humanum diceret, id est facile tractabile, et quod causarum comparatione mitescat. Non a vobis, inquit, reposco parem augustis rebus intentionem nec, quam magnae sunt virtutum opes, tam nova vobis, quibus eas capessatis, praecepta constituo, nihil ferum ingero, nihil quod vix portari possit indico, ne, si pro splendore iustitiae tale aliquid imperarem, de carnis infirmitate conquesti allegaretis iugem vos laborem ferre non posse. Nunc itaque hac moderatione convenio, ut tale studium virtutibus adhibeatis, quale adhibuistis ante criminibus; cumque iniuria sit honestarum rerum, si tali appetantur proposito, quale est deformibus impensum rebus, tamen disciplinae huic, in qua estis, sufficit, si vel tali intentione iustitiam sectemini, quali iniquitatem estis immunditiamque sectati.
pass_a_gloss: For lest he seem to command anything arduous and inaccessible to a human being, he usurped a word from custom, so that he would say human, that is easily tractable, and what grows mild by a comparison of causes. I do not, he says, demand from you an intention equal to august things, nor do I constitute for you precepts so new by which you may seize them as great as are the resources of virtues, I thrust in nothing wild, I indicate nothing which can scarcely be carried, lest, if I commanded anything of such a kind for the splendor of justice, having complained of the infirmity of the flesh you would allege that you cannot bear a continuous labor. Now therefore I convene by this moderation, that you apply such a pursuit to virtues as you applied before to crimes; and although it is an injury of honorable things if they are sought by such a purpose as has been expended on deformed things, nevertheless it suffices for this discipline in which you are, if you follow justice even by such an intention as you followed iniquity and uncleanness.

lemmas.lexica: LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: To avoid seeming to command anything arduous and inaccessible to a human being, he took an expression from ordinary speech and called it ‘human’: that is, easy to handle, something made gentler by comparing the cases. I do not demand of you, he says, an intensity matching these exalted realities; nor, great as virtue’s riches are, do I establish correspondingly novel commands by which you must obtain them. I impose nothing harsh, prescribe nothing barely bearable. If I commanded such a thing in proportion to righteousness’s splendor, you might complain of the flesh’s weakness and plead that you could not bear constant toil. So now I address you with this moderation: apply to virtues the same effort you previously applied to crimes. Although it insults honorable things to pursue them with merely the same determination spent on disgraceful things, it nevertheless suffices for your present training if you pursue righteousness with at least the intensity with which you pursued lawlessness and impurity.

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

choices.why: Scripture's destruction of iniquitas is the Law's purpose; keep moral injustice.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
